claim: GtACR1 from the alga Guillardia theta is a potent neuron-inhibiting optogenetics tool.
source: The anion channelrhodopsin GtACR1 from the alga Guillardia theta is a potent neuron-inhibiting optogenetics tool.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of GtACR1, supported by prior research and the current structural study.

claim: The X-ray structure of GtACR1 was determined at 2.9 Å resolution.
source: Presented here, its X-ray structure at 2.9 Å reveals a tunnel traversing the protein from its extracellular surface to a large cytoplasmic cavity.
evidence: The resolution is explicitly stated in the abstract and confirmed in Table 1 showing crystallographic data.

claim: GtACR1 contains a tunnel traversing the protein from its extracellular surface to a large cytoplasmic cavity.
source: Presented here, its X-ray structure at 2.9 Å reveals a tunnel traversing the protein from its extracellular surface to a large cytoplasmic cavity.
evidence: The tunnel is described in the abstract and visualized in Figure 2A and 2B showing cross-sections of the structure.

claim: The tunnel in GtACR1 is lined primarily by small polar and aliphatic residues essential for anion conductance.
source: The tunnel is lined primarily by small polar and aliphatic residues essential for anion conductance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A disulfide-immobilized extracellular cap facilitates channel closing in GtACR1.
source: A disulfide-immobilized extracellular cap facilitates channel closing and the ion path is blocked mid-membrane by its photoactive retinylidene chromophore and further by a cytoplasmic side constriction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 3C showing that disrupting the disulfide bridge slows channel closing.

claim: The ion path in GtACR1 is blocked mid-membrane by its photoactive retinylidene chromophore.
source: A disulfide-immobilized extracellular cap facilitates channel closing and the ion path is blocked mid-membrane by its photoactive retinylidene chromophore and further by a cytoplasmic side constriction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing the retinal position in the tunnel (Figure 2).

claim: The ion path in GtACR1 is blocked by a cytoplasmic side constriction.
source: A disulfide-immobilized extracellular cap facilitates channel closing and the ion path is blocked mid-membrane by its photoactive retinylidene chromophore and further by a cytoplasmic side constriction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis showing constriction C3 in Figure 2D and 3F.

claim: GtACR1 has a novel photoactive site configuration that maintains the retinylidene Schiff base protonated when the channel is open.
source: The structure also reveals a novel photoactive site configuration that maintains the retinylidene Schiff base protonated when the channel is open.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis in Figure 5A and prior photochemical studies cited in the text (Sineshchekov et al., 2016; Wietek et al., 2016).

claim: The Schiff base in GtACR1 controls gating and serves as a direct mediator for anion flux.
source: These findings suggest a new channelrhodopsin mechanism, in which the Schiff base not only controls gating, but also serves as a direct mediator for anion flux.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on structural findings and is supported by the location of the protonated Schiff base in the ion path.

claim: Anion channelrhodopsins (ACRs) are natural light-gated anion channels first discovered in the cryptophyte alga Guillardia theta.
source: Anion channelrhodopsins (ACRs) are natural light-gated anion channels first discovered in the cryptophyte alga Guillardia theta (GtACR1 and GtACR2) (Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: GtACRs have large Cl- conductance making them the most potent neuron-silencing optogenetic tools available.
source: Their large Cl- conductance makes GtACRs and other ACRs later found in various cryptophyte species (Govorunova et al., 2018; Govorunova et al., 2017b) the most potent neuron-silencing optogenetic tools available.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to studies demonstrating their effectiveness.

claim: GtACRs have been effective inhibitors of neural processes and behavior in flies, worms, zebrafish, ferrets, and mice.
source: GtACRs have proven to be effective inhibitors of neural processes and behavior in flies (Mauss et al., 2017; Mohammad et al., 2017; Steck et al., 2018), worms (Bergs et al., 2018), zebrafish (Mohamed et al., 2017), ferrets (Wilson et al., 2018), and mice (Forli et al., 2018; Mahn et al., 2018; Messier et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to studies in different organisms.

claim: GtACR1 is the best characterized ACR in terms of its gating mechanism and photochemical reaction cycle.
source: Of the 35 ACR homologs found in cryptophyte algae (Govorunova et al., 2018; Govorunova et al., 2016; Wietek et al., 2016), GtACR1 is the best characterized in terms of its gating mechanism and photochemical reaction cycle (Sineshchekov et al., 2015; Sineshchekov et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: GtACR1 is the only ACR for which light-gated anion conductance has been proven to be maintained in vitro in a purified state.
source: and also is the only ACR for which light-gated anion conductance has been proven to be maintained in vitro in a purified state (Li et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to the study demonstrating this property.

claim: ACRs conduct only anions with complete exclusion of cations, even H+.
source: The two channelrhodopsin families exhibit large differences in their sequences and photochemistry (Govorunova et al., 2017a): (i) ACRs conduct only anions with complete exclusion of cations, even H+, for which CCRs exhibit their highest relative permeability
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key difference between ACRs and CCRs, supported by citation.

claim: GtACR1 exhibits 25-fold higher unitary conductance than CrChR2.
source: (ii) ACRs are generally more potent; for example GtACR1 exhibits 25-fold higher unitary conductance than CrChR2
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a comparison between ACRs and CCRs.

claim: In ACRs, the retinylidene Schiff base remains protonated throughout the lifetime of the open-channel state.
source: (iii) The retinylidene Schiff base in the photoactive site deprotonates prior to channel opening in CCRs (Lórenz-Fonfría and Heberle, 2014) and, in contrast, in ACRs remains protonated throughout the lifetime of the open-channel state with deprotonation correlated with the initial phase of channel closing (Sineshchekov et al., 2016; Wietek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to studies demonstrating this property.

claim: In ACRs, Schiff base deprotonation is correlated with the initial phase of channel closing.
source: in ACRs remains protonated throughout the lifetime of the open-channel state with deprotonation correlated with the initial phase of channel closing (Sineshchekov et al., 2016; Wietek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to studies demonstrating this timing.

claim: GtACR1 protein was expressed in insect (Sf9) cells and purified as a disulfide-crosslinked homodimer.
source: The GtACR1 protein was expressed in insect (Sf9) cells and purified as a disulfide-crosslinked homodimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LCP crystals of GtACR1 were obtained and the structure was determined at 2.9 Å resolution using molecular replacement.
source: We obtained lipidic cubic phase (LCP) crystals of GtACR1, applied the continuous grid-scan method (Wojdyla et al., 2016) for X-ray data collection, and determined the structure at 2.9 Å resolution using molecular replacement (Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to the figure and table showing crystallographic data.

claim: Each asymmetric unit of the GtACR1 crystal contains a homodimer molecule.
source: Each asymmetric unit contains a GtACR1 homodimer molecule (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the crystal packing.

claim: Each GtACR1 monomer is composed of an extracellular cap domain, seven transmembrane helices (TM1-7), and a cytoplasmic loop at the carboxyl-terminus.
source: Each monomer is composed of an extracellular cap domain, seven transmembrane helices (TM1-7), and a cytoplasmic loop at the carboxyl-terminus (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The GtACR1 homodimer is stabilized by TM3 and TM4 interactions between monomers and an intermolecular disulfide bridge formed by C6 residues.
source: The GtACR1 homodimer is stabilized by TM3 and TM4 interactions between monomers and further by an intermolecular disulfide bridge formed by the C6 residues (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The dimeric arrangement of GtACR1 creates a large funnel-shaped cytoplasmic cavity (~18 Å deep and ~28 Å wide).
source: Since TM5-7 are much longer than TM1-4, this dimeric arrangement creates a large funnel-shaped cytoplasmic cavity (~18 Å deep and ~28 Å wide).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural measurements.

claim: GtACR1 and C1C2/CrChR2 share ~24% amino acid sequence identity.
source: Despite the modest ~24% amino acid sequence identity between GtACR1 and C1C2/CrChR2, the structure of each GtACR1 protomer can be superposed well (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) with either of the two CCR structures (r.m.s.d. 0.9 Å)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between the structures.

claim: The structure of each GtACR1 protomer can be superposed with C1C2/CrChR2 structures with r.m.s.d. 0.9 Å.
source: Despite the modest ~24% amino acid sequence identity between GtACR1 and C1C2/CrChR2, the structure of each GtACR1 protomer can be superposed well (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) with either of the two CCR structures (r.m.s.d. 0.9 Å)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: GtACR1 and CCRs share a common TM helical scaffold conformation in their closed states.
source: indicating that these functionally distinct channelrhodopsins share a common TM helical scaffold conformation in their closed states.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural superposition.

claim: A continuous tunnel spanning through the protein from the extracellular to cytoplasmic surface was detected in each GtACR1 protomer by serial cross-sections.
source: A continuous tunnel spanning through the protein from the extracellular to cytoplasmic surface was detected in each GtACR1 protomer by serial cross-sections (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The tunnel in GtACR1 starts from an electropositive port on the extracellular surface, intersects the retinylidene Schiff base in the middle of the membrane, and ends at an intracellular port deeply embedded in the large dimeric cavity.
source: The tunnel, assembled by TM1-3 and 7, starts from an electropositive port on the extracellular surface, intersects the retinylidene Schiff base in the middle of the membrane, and ends at an intracellular port deeply embedded in the large dimeric cavity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The continuous intramolecular tunnel in GtACR1 was detected by the program CAVER with probe radius 0.9 Å.
source: The continuous intramolecular tunnel in GtACR1 directly visualized by cross-section, presumably indicating the anion conductance pathway, was also detected by the program CAVER (probe radius 0.9 Å) (Kozlikova et al., 2014) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to the computational method and figure.

claim: Only a partial tunnel open on the extracellular side was found in C1C2.
source: For comparison, only a partial tunnel open on the extracellular side was found in C1C2 (Kato et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation and reference to a figure showing the comparison.

claim: No tunnel open to either surface was found with CAVER in CrChR2.
source: and we found no tunnel open to either surface with CAVER in CrChR2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on computational analysis.

claim: The tunnel of GtACR1 is primarily lined by small polar and aliphatic residues in contrast to charged residues in corresponding positions in C1C2 and CrChR2.
source: Despite the high similarity of the TM helix scaffolds of GtACR1 and C1C2/CrChR2, the tunnel of GtACR1 is primarily lined by small polar and aliphatic residues (Figure 2C) in contrast to charged residues in the corresponding positions in C1C2 and CrChR2: A75 vs E136/E97 (C1C2/CrChR2 numbering), T71 vs K132/K93; S97 vs E162/E123, A61 vs E122/E83, and L108 vs H173/H134 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 top row).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures showing the residue differences.

claim: The differences in GtACR1 from the CCR structures significantly reduce the negativity of the putative channel pore lining consistent with anion vs. cation conductance.
source: The differences in GtACR1 from the CCR structures significantly reduce the negativity of the putative channel pore lining consistent with anion vs. cation conductance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural differences.

claim: An intraprotomer disulfide bridge is formed between C21 from the amino-terminal segment and C219 within the TM6-7 loop in GtACR1.
source: In addition to the disulfide link between the two protomers, an intraprotomer disulfide bridge is formed between C21 from the amino-terminal segment and C219 within the TM6-7 loop (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The intramolecular C21-C219 disulfide crosslink immobilizes the kinked helices to the retinal-conjugated TM7 and encaps a hydrophobic part of the segment on the extracellular tunnel entry port.
source: This intramolecular crosslink immobilizes the kinked helices to the retinal-conjugated TM7, and encaps a hydrophobic part of the segment on the extracellular tunnel entry port (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Disrupting the extracellular loop conformation by truncation of the amino-terminal loop (Δ1–25) or by substituting C21 and C219 with serine resulted in slowed channel closing.
source: Disrupting this extracellular loop conformation, either by truncation of the amino-terminal loop (Δ1–25) or by substituting C21 and C219 with serine to abolish the intramolecular disulfide, resulted in slowed channel closing (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C with photocurrent decay kinetics.

claim: Both C21 and C219 are highly conserved in ACRs but not in CCRs.
source: Both C21 and C219 are highly conserved in ACRs (Govorunova et al., 2017b), but not in CCRs, revealing a role of this intramolecular disulfide bridge specific to the ACR family.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to a study on ACR conservation.

claim: The intramolecular tunnel in GtACR1 is constricted at three positions: at the extracellular port (C1), near the photoactive retinylidene Schiff base (C2), and at the cytoplasmic side (C3).
source: The intramolecular tunnel in GtACR1 is constricted at three positions: at the extracellular port (C1), near the photoactive retinylidene Schiff base (C2), and at the cytoplasmic side (C3) (Figures 2D and 3D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2D and 3D-F.

claim: The C1 constriction is stabilized by an H-bond network formed by the side chains of Y81, R94 and E223.
source: Near the extracellular port, the C1 constriction (Figure 3D) is stabilized by an H-bond network adjacent to the disulfide-immobilized extracellular cap and formed by the side chains of Y81, R94 and E223 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: The mutation R94A nearly abolished Cl- conductance.
source: The mutation R94A nearly abolished Cl- conductance (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D with photocurrent measurements.

claim: Mutations R94A, E223Q, Y81F, and C21S_C219S strongly slowed the slow decay phase of channel closing to a similar extent.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and reported earlier for the E223Q mutant (Sineshchekov et al., 2015), all three mutations strongly slowed the slow decay phase to a similar extent as that observed in the C21S_C219S mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a prior study.

claim: The combination of the H-bond network of E223 and its neighbouring intraprotomer disulfide bridge controls the rate of channel closing in the extracellular region and stabilizes R94 in the closed state.
source: These results suggest that the combination of the H-bond network of E223 and its neighbouring intraprotomer disulfide bridge controls the rate of channel closing in the extracellular region and stabilizes the essential residue R94 in the closed state.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the mutagenesis data.

claim: The narrowest constriction C2 lies at the photoactive site and is formed by the side chains of T101, L64, and M105.
source: The narrowest constriction C2 lies at the photoactive site and is formed by the side chains of T101, L64, and M105 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Four of the five residues that form the intracellular constriction C3 (L108, A61, E60, L245 and P58) are in corresponding positions as the residues that form the 'intracellular gate' in CCRs.
source: Four of the five residues that form the intracellular constriction C3 (L108, A61, E60, L245 and P58) (Figure 3F) are in corresponding positions as the residues that form the 'intracellular gate' in CCRs (Deisseroth and Hegemann, 2017), but in GtACR1 and other ACRs only E60 (E121/E82) is shared with CCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation and reference to Figure 3F.

claim: Perturbation of any residues at C2 or C3 greatly reduced or eliminated the photocurrents, while effects of most mutations (except A75E) at the C1 position were negligible.
source: Indeed, perturbation of any residues at C2 or C3 greatly reduced or eliminated the photocurrents, while effects of most mutations (except A75E) at the C1 position were negligible (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G with photocurrent measurements.

claim: In the open conformation, the GtACR1 channel is wider in the extracellular portion and more narrow in its central and intracellular stretches.
source: suggesting that in the open conformation the channel is wider in the extracellular portion and more narrow in its central and intracellular stretches.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Mutations of the C1 and C3 residues mostly affected the slow phase of channel closing, making it slower than that in the wild-type.
source: Kinetically, the mutations of the C1 and C3 residues mostly affected the slow phase of channel closing, making it slower than that in the wild-type (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the tested mutants yielded Erev values that were statistically significantly different from the wild type under Cl- gradient conditions.
source: None of the mutants in which photocurrents near the reversal potential could be resolved from the background noise yielded Erev values that were statistically significantly different from that measured in the wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; full statistical results are in Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures and statistical analysis in Table 2.

claim: Seven tested single and double mutants showed no shift in Erev under Cl- gradient conditions from the Cl- Nernst potential.
source: However, we found no such change when we tested seven of these single and double mutants (Figure 3—figure supplements 5 and 6; full statistical results are in Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures and statistical analysis.

claim: The tested mutants showed no statistically significant difference from the wild type in the presence of H+ and Na+ gradients.
source: Therefore, we further tested these mutants in the presence of H+ and Na+ gradients (Figure 3—figure supplements 7 and 8, respectively) and again found no statistically significant difference from the wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 9; full statistical results are in Tables 3 and 4), indicating that none of these mutations produced permeability for these cations in GtACR1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures and statistical analysis in Tables 3 and 4.

claim: The unphotolyzed state of GtACR1 contains almost exclusively all-trans retinal.
source: Confocal near-infrared resonance Raman spectroscopy has shown that the unphotolyzed state of GtACR1 contains almost exclusively all-trans retinal (Yi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to a spectroscopy study.

claim: The presence of F160 in GtACR1 pushes the β-ionone ring towards the extracellular side by 1.2 Å compared to C1C2/CrChR2.
source: While the conformations of the retinal polyene chain are nearly identical in GtACR1 and C1C2/CrChR2, the presence of F160 in GtACR1 (G224/G185 in C1C2/CrChR2, respectively) pushes the β-ionone ring towards the extracellular side by 1.2 Å (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The action spectrum of photocurrents generated by the F160G mutant was almost identical to that of the wild-type GtACR1.
source: Despite this conformational difference, the action spectrum of photocurrents generated by the F160G mutant was almost identical to that of the wild-type GtACR1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In C1C2 and CrChR2, the protonated Schiff base participates in a quadruple salt-bridge network formed with D292/D253, E162/E123 and K132/K93 sidechains.
source: In C1C2 and CrChR2 the protonated Schiff base (PSB) participates in a quadruple salt-bridge network formed with D292/D253, E162/E123 and K132/K93 sidechains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The strong salt-bridge network around the Schiff base is absent in the GtACR1 structure due to the replacement of E162/E123 and K132/K93 with smaller uncharged residues S97 and T71.
source: However, this strong network is absent in the GtACR1 structure due to the replacement of E162/E123 and K132/K93 with smaller uncharged residues S97 and T71, respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: D234 is the only residue directly interacting with the protonated Schiff base in GtACR1.
source: D234 is the only residue directly interacting with the protonated Schiff base (PSB) in GtACR1, and its electrostatic interaction appears to be weakened by two H-bonds from tyrosine residues Y72 and Y207 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The electrostatic interaction of D234 with the Schiff base appears to be weakened by two H-bonds from tyrosine residues Y72 and Y207.
source: D234 is the only residue directly interacting with the protonated Schiff base (PSB) in GtACR1, and its electrostatic interaction appears to be weakened by two H-bonds from tyrosine residues Y72 and Y207 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In bacteriorhodopsin, tyrosinyl H-bond-weakened interactions of D212 prevent it from accepting the Schiff base proton, which is transferred instead to D85 in the proton release pathway.
source: The proton pump bacteriorhodopsin exhibits similar tyrosinyl H-bond-weakened interactions of D212, the residue in the corresponding position as D234. The interactions prevent D212 from accepting the Schiff base proton, which is transferred instead to D85 in the proton release pathway (Luecke et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to a study on bacteriorhodopsin structure.

claim: Resonance Raman and UV-vis absorption spectra of the D234N mutant of GtACR1 indicate that D234 is neutral and not a Schiff base proton acceptor.
source: Resonance Raman and UV-vis absorption spectra of the D234N mutant of GtACR1 indicate that D234 is similarly neutral and not a Schiff base proton acceptor (Sineshchekov et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to spectroscopy studies.

claim: The dark structure may explain the persistence of protonation of the Schiff base throughout the lifetime of the open channel conformation in GtACR1.
source: The dark structure therefore may explain the persistence of protonation of the Schiff base throughout the lifetime of the open channel conformation in GtACR1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural findings.

claim: Y207 appeared to be more important functionally than Y72, as its replacement with phenylalanine suppressed the photocurrents to a greater extent.
source: Of the two tyrosine residues, Y207 appeared to be more important functionally, as its replacement with phenylalanine suppressed the photocurrents to a greater extent than that of Y72 (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D with photocurrent measurements.

claim: The Y207F mutation caused a 12 nm blue shift of the action spectrum.
source: and caused a 12 nm blue shift of the action spectrum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Y72F mutation mostly affected the slow decay phase, while the Y207F mutation caused a strong perturbation of both phases.
source: The Y72F mutation mostly affected the slow decay phase, while the Y207F mutation caused a strong perturbation of both phases (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In CrChR2, photoisomerization of the Schiff base rapidly disrupts the strong salt-bridged network by inducing transfer of the Schiff base proton to D253 or E123 in ~10 µs prior to channel opening.
source: In CrChR2, photoisomerization of the Schiff base rapidly disrupts the strong salt-bridged network by inducing transfer of the Schiff base proton to D253 or E123 in ~10 µs prior to channel opening (Lórenz-Fonfría and Heberle, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to a study on CrChR2 photochemistry.

claim: In GtACR1, the Schiff base remains protonated throughout the lifetime of the open channel conformation, and deprotonation occurs late in the photocycle (~20 ms) correlated with fast channel closing.
source: In contrast, the Schiff base remains protonated throughout the lifetime of the open channel conformation in GtACR1, and deprotonation of the Schiff base proton occurs late in the photocycle (~20 ms) correlated with fast channel closing (Sineshchekov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to a prior study.

claim: In GtACR1, no immediate proton accepting residue is available in the vicinity of the PSB and later structural changes are required to enable Schiff base proton transfer, possibly to E68.
source: Unlike in the salt-bridge network around the Schiff base in the CCRs (Figure 5B), in GtACR1 no immediate proton accepting residue is available in the vicinity of the PSB and therefore later structural changes are required to enable Schiff base proton transfer, possibly to E68 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural findings.

claim: The location of the PSB, centered within the anion path in GtACR1, suggests that it may play a direct role in anion translocation in the open channel state.
source: The location of the PSB, centered within the anion path in GtACR1, suggests that it may play a direct role in anion translocation in the open channel state.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on the structural findings.

claim: The PSB is only partially neutralized by its D234 counterion because the counterion is weakened by its interaction with the two tyrosinyl residues.
source: Consistent with this idea is that the PSB is only partially neutralized by its D234 counterion because the counterion is weakened by its interaction with the two tyrosinyl residues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural findings.

claim: The PSB presents a partial positive charge capable of transient reversible interaction with Cl- ions in a channel that is largely lined by small polar and hydrophobic aliphatic residues.
source: Therefore, the PSB presents a partial positive charge capable of transient reversible interaction with Cl- ions in a channel that is largely lined by small polar and hydrophobic aliphatic residues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the structural findings.

claim: Late deprotonation of the Schiff base after channel opening occurs in all three ACRs examined: GtACR1, GtACR2, and PsuACR1.
source: Supporting a possible direct role of the PSB in the channel's permeability for anions, late deprotonation of the Schiff base after channel opening occurs in all three ACRs so far examined: GtACR1 and GtACR2 (Sineshchekov et al., 2016) and PsuACR1 (Wietek et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to studies on different ACRs.

claim: Schiff base deprotonation after channel opening is not known to occur in any CCR.
source: yet Schiff base deprotonation after channel opening is not known to occur in any CCR.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a contrast to ACRs.

claim: The mutant S97E exhibits appearance of fast Schiff base deprotonation and a > 30 fold suppression of the amplitude of the chloride photocurrent.
source: Further indicating an essential role of the protonated Schiff base form, the mutant S97E, in which a potential Schiff base proton acceptor is placed at the corresponding position in GtACR1 as in CCRs and many other microbial rhodopsins, exhibits (i) appearance of fast Schiff base deprotonation, and (ii) a > 30 fold suppression of the amplitude of the chloride photocurrent (Sineshchekov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to a prior study.

claim: The double mutation Y207F/Y72F decreased the photocurrent amplitude to a negligible value.
source: Furthermore, the double mutation Y207F/Y72F, expected to release inhibition of D234 as a proton acceptor, decreased the photocurrent amplitude to a negligible value (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D with photocurrent measurements.

claim: E68 forms an H-bond network with N239 and S43 in GtACR1.
source: E68, a glutamyl residue near the Schiff base constriction in the channel, forms an H-bond network with N239 and S43 (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ENS triad in GtACR1 has a geometry similar to that of a homologous triad (E129/E90, N297/N258, and S102/S63) referred to as 'the central gate' in C1C2 and CrChR2.
source: with a geometry similar to that of a homologous triad (E129/E90, N297/N258, and S102/S63) referred to as 'the central gate' in C1C2 and CrChR2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a structural comparison.

claim: In C1C2 and CrChR2, the triad blocks the cation path from the extracellular bulk phase.

claim: The two GtACR1 structures (6EDQ and 6CSM) show an extremely high similarity with a marginal RMSD value of ~0.4 Å.

However, they were obtained in different crystallization conditions and exhibit different space groups and crystal packing. Nevertheless, the two show an extremely high similarity with a marginal RMSD value of ~0.4 Å.
